As of December 31, 2023, Boeing reported these shares of its total workforce:

- **33%** — employees represented by labor unions overall.
- **21%** — employees represented by the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM).
- **10%** — employees represented by the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (SPEEA).
- **1%** — employees represented by the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW).

The union-specific percentages are subsets of the overall figure. Boeing reported approximately 57,000 union-represented employees. [Boeing 2023 Form 10-K, pp. 2, 9](BA_2023_10K.pdf)

ExxonMobil’s 2025 Form 10-K reports the following **year-end capacity** for its 100%-owned Huizhou complex:

- **1.6 million metric tons per year** of ethylene.
- **1.7 million metric tons per year** of polyethylene.
- **0.9 million metric tons per year** of polypropylene.

The filing also says the complex’s three polyethylene and two polypropylene production lines have a **combined capacity of over 2.5 million metric tons per year**. That figure covers the polymer lines, not ethylene capacity. [Source: 2025 Form 10-K, pp. 21 and 51; PDF pp. 23 and 53.]

ExxonMobil attributes the sharp rise in 2022 refining margins to a **tight market** caused by recovering demand and constrained supply:

- **Fuel demand recovered:** Gasoline and diesel demand returned to pre-pandemic levels, although jet fuel demand remained below historical levels.
- **Refining capacity fell:** Refinery shutdowns and reduced investment during the pandemic curtailed industry capacity. The filing says more than 3 million barrels per day of capacity had been taken offline.
- **Supply chains and inventories were strained:** Supply-chain constraints and low inventories added to the tightness as demand recovered.

The company says margins rose well above the top of their 2010–2019 historical range. [ExxonMobil 2022 Form 10-K, pp. 47, 53–54](XOM_2022_10K.pdf)

The filing attributes PCC’s revenue decline to reduced aircraft production in 2021 and 2020. The COVID-19 pandemic caused material declines in commercial air travel and aircraft production; airlines delayed or canceled orders, and companies across the industry reduced inventories. [Form 10-K, p. K-49](BRK_2022_10K.pdf#page=51)

More broadly, Berkshire says the sudden, substantial drop in air travel led manufacturers to cut aircraft build rates and customers to draw down inventories at extraordinary rates. Production delays in Boeing’s 737 MAX and 787 programs also adversely affected PCC’s aerospace business. [Form 10-K, p. K-12](BRK_2022_10K.pdf#page=14)

Apple identified four results that were unfavorably affected year over year by currency weakness against the U.S. dollar:

- **Greater China net sales:** The weaker renminbi contributed to an unfavorable impact. Sales fell from $72.6 billion in 2023 to $67.0 billion in 2024.
- **Japan net sales:** The weaker yen had an unfavorable impact, although sales rose from $24.3 billion to $25.1 billion.
- **Rest of Asia Pacific net sales:** Weakness in foreign currencies had a net unfavorable impact, although sales rose from $29.6 billion to $30.7 billion. [Apple 2024 Form 10-K, p. 22](AAPL_2024_10K.pdf#page=25)
- **Products gross margin and gross margin percentage:** Foreign-currency weakness partially offset cost savings. Both measures nevertheless increased: gross margin rose from $108.8 billion to $109.6 billion, and gross margin percentage rose from 36.5% to 37.2%. [Apple 2024 Form 10-K, p. 24](AAPL_2024_10K.pdf#page=27)

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2023 Form 10-K describes four effects of the war and the measures imposed in response:

- **Blocked deliveries:** Sanctions and export controls blocked NVIDIA’s products, services and support from entering Russia, Belarus and certain regions of Ukraine. [p. 28]
- **Exit from Russia:** NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia and later closed its Russian business operations during fiscal 2023. Direct sales to Russia had been immaterial in fiscal 2022. [pp. 28, 37]
- **End-customer sales:** The war had affected end-customer sales in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). [p. 28]
- **Partner revenue:** Revenue from partners that sell into Russia **may have been negatively affected** by the war. NVIDIA did not state this effect as certain. [p. 37]

The filing did not quantify the war’s effect on EMEA sales or partner revenue.

Boeing’s 2025 Form 10-K gives four percentages:

| Percentage | Revenue or backlog amount |
|---|---|
| **46%** | Boeing’s total 2025 revenue was attributable to non-U.S. customers. |
| **60%** | Commercial Airplanes’ 2025 revenue from customer contracts was attributable to non-U.S. customers. |
| **Approximately 85%** | Commercial Airplanes’ total backlog, in dollar terms, was with non-U.S. airlines. |
| **26%** | Defense, Space & Security’s backlog at December 31, 2025 was attributable to non-U.S. customers. |

For the two revenue figures, non-U.S. customers include Foreign Military Sales through the U.S. government. Sources: [Boeing 2025 Form 10-K, pp. 10, 33 and 38](BA_2025_10K.pdf).

NVIDIA says these securities are investments in private companies without readily determinable fair values. Valuation is inherently complex because market data and observable transactions are not readily available, and macroeconomic factors affect values.

As a result, adjustments can require unobservable inputs, including volatility, expected time to liquidity, the risk-free rate, and rights and obligations specific to each security. NVIDIA also assesses impairment using qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee’s operating performance and market trends. [NVIDIA fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, pp. 38, 45, 66–67]

Walmart’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K reports these long-term debt repayments, in **millions of U.S. dollars**:

- **$3,468** — total repayments of long-term debt in the cash-flow statement and debt rollforward. [pp. 44, 57]
- **$3,373** — total repayments of the significant matured debt listed in Note 6, comprising: [p. 69]
  - **$1,500** — debt maturing April 22, 2024.
  - **$990** — debt maturing July 8, 2024.
  - **$253** — repayment of ¥40,000 million in debt maturing July 18, 2024.
  - **$630** — debt maturing December 15, 2024.

The $3,373 is part of the $3,468 total, not an additional repayment.

The filing cites three offsets to production growth:

- **Divestments** of production assets;
- **Russia’s expropriation** of ExxonMobil’s interests; and
- **Lower production entitlements due to higher prices.** At higher prices, fewer barrels are needed to recover costs under certain contractual arrangements.

Growth in the Permian and Guyana, together with easing government-mandated curtailments, more than offset those impacts. Overall production rose by 25,000 oil-equivalent barrels per day from 2021. [ExxonMobil 2022 Form 10-K, p. 52](XOM_2022_10K.pdf#page=54)

Berkshire’s 2024 Form 10-K gives the following affiliate-borrowing amounts, excluding interest:

| Operating business | Amounts in billions |
|---|---|
| **Clayton Homes** | Affiliate borrowings **increased by $6.6 billion** during 2024, reaching **$24.3 billion** at December 31, 2024. [p. K-48] |
| **Pilot Travel Centers** | Pilot **borrowed $5.7 billion** from Berkshire insurance subsidiaries in March 2024 to repay third-party borrowings, then **repaid $1.0 billion** of the affiliate borrowings during 2024. [p. K-53] |

Source: Berkshire Hathaway, *2024 Form 10-K*, pp. K-48 and K-53.

Pfizer’s 2021 Form 10-K gives the following figures for Upjohn separation costs:

- **Approximately $700 million** — the total costs Pfizer expected to incur in separating Upjohn, including legal-entity separation and transaction costs.
- **Approximately 75%** — the portion of that expected total incurred from inception through December 31, 2021. [Form 10-K, p. 26](PFE_2021_10K.pdf#page=32)
- **$434 million in 2020 and $83 million in 2019** — separation-related costs Pfizer incurred in those respective years and included in discontinued operations, net of tax. They primarily related to professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities, as well as investment banking fees. [Form 10-K, p. 65](PFE_2021_10K.pdf#page=71)

Walmart’s fiscal 2022 Form 10-K gives these counts:

| Scope | Pickup locations | Delivery locations |
|---|---:|---:|
| **Global business** | “over 8,000” | “6,000” |
| **Walmart U.S. segment** | “approximately 4,600” | “more than 3,500” **same-day** delivery locations |
| **Walmart International segment** | “approximately 2,900” | “over 1,900” |

The filing states the global figures together as “**over 8,000 pickup and 6,000 delivery locations globally**.” The segment figures are as of January 31, 2022. The U.S. delivery count specifically covers **same-day delivery**; the global and International counts are described as delivery locations without that qualifier. [Walmart fiscal 2022 Form 10-K, pp. 6–7, 9]

Walmart’s fiscal 2026 filing gives these causes for the gross profit rate increases, compared with fiscal 2025:

- **Company-wide: up 8 basis points.** The increase was primarily driven by disciplined inventory management at Walmart U.S. and growth in higher-margin businesses globally. [Form 10-K, p. 35]
- **Walmart U.S.: up 22 basis points.** The segment cited disciplined inventory management and growth in higher-margin businesses. [p. 39]
- **Sam’s Club U.S.: up 4 basis points.** The segment cited operational efficiencies and higher fuel margins. [p. 41]

Walmart International’s gross profit rate decreased in fiscal 2026, so it is not included. [p. 40]

Walmart attributed the fiscal 2025 increases to the following factors, compared with fiscal 2024:

- **Company-wide:** The operating expense ratio rose **36 basis points**, primarily because of higher variable pay after performance exceeded plan, increased marketing, and higher depreciation expenses. [Form 10-K, p. 39](WMT_2025_10K.pdf#page=39)
- **Walmart U.S.:** The ratio rose **44 basis points**, primarily because of increased marketing expenses, higher variable pay after exceeding planned performance, and increased depreciation expenses. [p. 40](WMT_2025_10K.pdf#page=40)
- **Sam’s Club U.S.:** The ratio rose **44 basis points**, primarily because of increased compensation-related expenses—including investments in associate wages and higher variable pay after exceeding planned performance—and elevated technology spending. [p. 42](WMT_2025_10K.pdf#page=42)

Walmart International’s ratio **fell** by 5 basis points, so it was not one of the segments with an increase. [p. 41](WMT_2025_10K.pdf#page=41)

Pfizer says the increase primarily reflected **$8.0 billion of IPR&D assets acquired with Metsera**. That addition was partly offset by **$3.9 billion of IPR&D impairments** and transfers from IPR&D to developed technology rights: $600 million for Padcev and $590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna). [Pfizer 2025 Form 10-K, Note 10, p. 83](PFE_2025_10K.pdf#page=93)

Pfizer attributes the impairment charges primarily to changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts. The IPR&D charges included $1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin, $820 million for Tukysa (tucatinib), and $820 million for osivelotor. [Note 4, p. 70](PFE_2025_10K.pdf#page=79)

Apple’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K gives these percentages:

| Measure | Percentage | What it represents |
|---|---:|---|
| Fiscal 2025 net sales | **40%** | Sales through Apple’s direct distribution channels, including its stores and direct sales force. |
| Fiscal 2025 net sales | **60%** | Sales through indirect channels, such as third-party cellular carriers and other resellers. |
| Trade receivables at September 27, 2025 | **12%** | The share attributable to one customer. |
| Trade receivables at September 27, 2025 | **34%** | The share attributable to third-party cellular network carriers collectively. |
| Vendor non-trade receivables at September 27, 2025 | **46% and 23%** | The respective shares attributable to two individual manufacturing vendors. These receivables arose from components Apple sold to the vendors. |

The receivables percentages have different denominators: the first two use **total trade receivables**, while the last two use **total vendor non-trade receivables**. The filing does not identify the individual customer or vendors in these disclosures. [Apple 2025 Form 10-K, pp. 2 and 39](AAPL_2025_10K.pdf)

As of January 31, 2026, Walmart reported these amounts for its cross-currency swaps:

- **$6,020 million:** The swaps’ notional amount—the reference amount used for the contracts, not their fair value. [Form 10-K, p. 69]
- **$(920) million:** Their aggregate fair value, a liability. Walmart also stated this as **$0.9 billion**. The fair value represents the estimated amount payable upon termination of the agreements at the reporting date. [pp. 47, 69]
- **$0.7 billion:** The hypothetical change in the swaps’ value if the U.S. dollar uniformly weakened by 10% against the underlying currencies. [p. 47]
- **$0.1 billion:** The hypothetical change in the swaps’ value from a 10% change in their underlying interest rates from the rates in effect at year-end. [p. 47]

Pfizer attributed the approximately **$1.1 billion favorable change** primarily to net gains on equity securities in 2023, compared with net losses in 2022, and lower net interest expense. Higher intangible-asset impairment charges partly offset those improvements. [Pfizer 2023 Form 10-K, p. 40]

Net equity-security results shifted from a **$1.273 billion loss** in 2022 to a **$1.590 billion gain** in 2023. The 2023 gains included a $1.7 billion realized gain on Telavant and a $297 million unrealized gain on Cerevel, partly offset by a $292 million unrealized loss on BioNTech. The 2022 losses included $986 million in unrealized losses on BioNTech, Allogene and Arvinas investments.

Net interest expense fell from **$987 million to $585 million**. Interest expense rose, driven by the $31 billion of senior unsecured notes issued in May 2023 to help finance the Seagen acquisition. More than offsetting that increase was higher interest income earned by investing the net proceeds of the debt issuance.

The principal offset was higher asset impairments: **$3.024 billion in 2023 versus $421 million in 2022**. The 2023 charges included $1.4 billion for Velsipity in-process research and development, reflecting changed development plans and revenue expectations, and $964 million for Prevnar 13 technology rights, reflecting updated forecasts and a transition to higher serotype coverage. [Note 4, p. 73]

ExxonMobil gives four annual dollar sensitivities in its 2025 Form 10-K:

| Change | Stated annual effect |
|---|---|
| **Brent crude:** $1 per barrel | Approximately **$700 million** after tax on Upstream earnings |
| **Henry Hub natural gas:** $0.10 per million metric British thermal units (MMBtu) | Approximately **$90 million** after tax on Upstream earnings |
| **Title Transfer Facility (TTF) natural gas:** $0.10 per MMBtu | Approximately **$20 million** after tax on Upstream earnings |
| **Worldwide pension assumption:** 0.5 percentage-point reduction in the long-term expected return on plan assets | Approximately **$150 million increase** in pension expense before tax |

The commodity sensitivities are for **2026**, include consolidated and equity-company Upstream earnings, and exclude derivatives. ExxonMobil cautions that benchmark changes are only broad indicators of actual earnings effects. The Brent sensitivity includes oil-linked LNG sales; the TTF sensitivity primarily represents LNG sales. [ExxonMobil 2025 Form 10-K, pp. 62, 67](XOM_2025_10K.pdf)

Pfizer’s 2024 Form 10-K gives these Haleon ownership figures:

| Point in time | Pfizer’s ownership |
|---|---:|
| December 31, 2023 | **32%** |
| After the March 2024 share sale | **Approximately 23%** |
| After the October 2024 sale, as of December 31, 2024 | **Approximately 15%** |
| After an additional sale in the first quarter of 2025 | **Approximately 7%** |

The filing also says Pfizer sold approximately **30% of its investment** in March 2024 and **34% of its remaining investment** in October. Those are portions of Pfizer’s holdings sold, not percentages of Haleon owned. [Pfizer 2024 Form 10-K, pp. 47, 66; PDF pp. 56, 75]

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2024 Form 10-K gives these amounts:

- **$2.2 billion** in total provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations. [p. 40]
- **$774 million** in inventory provisions recorded in cost of revenue. [p. 68]
- **Approximately $1.4 billion** in cost-of-revenue expense for inventory purchase obligations exceeding current demand projections, supplier charges, and penalties for cancellations and underutilization. [p. 70]
- **$540 million in provision releases** resulting from sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations. [p. 40]

The $774 million and approximately $1.4 billion amounts describe parts of the broader charges, not additional charges to add to the $2.2 billion total.

The 2021 Form 10-K identifies three projects as funded in 2021:

- **Bacalhau Phase 1, Brazil** — funded in 2021; ExxonMobil announced its final investment decision in June 2021. [pp. 16, 46](XOM_2021_10K.pdf)
- **North Field Production Sustainment Integrated Drilling and Looping, Qatar** — funded in 2021. [p. 17](XOM_2021_10K.pdf)
- **Jansz-Io Compression, Australia** — funded in 2021 as part of the Gorgon Jansz LNG development. [p. 18](XOM_2021_10K.pdf)

The filing also reports a final investment decision for a **chemical complex in Huizhou, China**, under “Key Recent Events,” but does not explicitly date that decision in the passage. [p. 53](XOM_2021_10K.pdf)

Boeing’s 2022 Form 10-K reports the following shares of 2022 revenue from fixed-price contracts:

- **Commercial Airplanes (BCA): 100%**
- **Defense, Space & Security (BDS): 60%**
- **Global Services (BGS), overall: 88%**
- **BGS defense business: approximately 69%**

The 69% figure applies specifically to BGS’s defense business, while 88% applies to the BGS segment overall. [Boeing 2022 Form 10-K, pp. 13, 111–112](BA_2022_10K.pdf)

Walmart identified the following fiscal 2024 improvements as benefiting, at least in part, from comparisons with fiscal 2023 charges or markdowns:

| Fiscal 2024 result | Fiscal 2023 item lapped |
|---|---|
| **Consolidated gross profit rate**, up 27 basis points | Higher markdowns, primarily in Walmart U.S. |
| **Walmart U.S. gross profit rate**, up 20 basis points | Higher net markdowns. |
| **Sam’s Club gross profit rate**, up 55 basis points | Elevated markdowns. |
| **Consolidated operating expenses as a percentage of net sales**, down 60 basis points | $3.3 billion of opioid-related legal settlement charges and $0.8 billion of Walmart International reorganization and restructuring charges. |
| **Walmart International operating expenses as a percentage of segment sales**, down 152 basis points | Business reorganization and restructuring charges related to Flipkart and Massmart. |
| **Return on investment**, up from 12.7% to 15.0% | Opioid-related legal settlement and reorganization and restructuring charges, through higher operating income. |

The filing also attributes several results to the factors above, rather than separately restating the lapping items:

- **Consolidated operating income margin**, up 83 basis points, and **consolidated net income**, up $5.0 billion, reflected the consolidated gross-margin and expense factors, among others.
- **Walmart U.S. operating income**, up $1.5 billion, reflected its gross-margin factors, including the lapped markdowns.
- **Walmart International operating income**, up $1.9 billion, reflected its expense factors, including the lapped restructuring charges.
- **Sam’s Club operating income**, up $0.2 billion, reflected its gross-margin factors, including the lapped markdowns.

The filing discusses some consolidated results twice; they are counted only once here. Other factors also affected each result. [Walmart fiscal 2024 Form 10-K, pp. 38, 41–44](WMT_2024_10K.pdf)

The increase reflected the transfer of certain First Republic deposits from Consumer & Community Banking to Asset & Wealth Management in the fourth quarter of 2023, as well as growth in balances in new and existing client accounts, including the impact of higher-yielding product offerings. [JPMorgan Chase 2024 Form 10-K, pp. 55–56, 64, 84](JPM_2024_10K.pdf)

Boeing’s 2024 Form 10-K gives four dividend amounts for the Series A preferred stock:

- **$345 million per year:** The maximum cash Boeing expected to need annually for dividends on the outstanding shares through the October 15, 2027 mandatory conversion date. (p. 17)
- **$58 million:** Preferred dividends accumulated during 2024, deducted in calculating net loss attributable to common shareholders. (p. 54)
- **$72 million:** The dividend declared in December 2024 and paid in cash on January 15, 2025. (pp. 58, 106)
- **$12.50 per preferred share:** The per-share amount of that declared dividend. (p. 106)

The $58 million accumulated in 2024 and the $72 million declared dividend are different measures: the latter covers the full declared payment, not just the amount accumulated during 2024.

Apple’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K identifies four developments dated to a specific day or month in calendar 2025:

- **April 23 — EU Digital Markets Act investigations:** The European Commission fined Apple **€500 million** in its Article 5(4) investigation and ordered it to remove restrictions preventing developers from steering users to alternatives outside the App Store. Apple appealed. The Commission also issued preliminary findings that day in a separate Article 6(4) investigation into Apple’s contractual requirements for third-party developers and app marketplaces. [Item 3, p. 18](AAPL_2025_10K.pdf#page=21)
- **April 30 — Epic Games litigation:** A California district court found Apple in violation of its 2021 injunction. It barred Apple from imposing fees on certain purchases outside apps and from restricting developers’ guidance to consumers or interfering with consumers’ choice to proceed in or out of an app. The court also denied Apple’s motion to narrow or vacate the injunction and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for consideration of criminal contempt proceedings. Apple appealed. [Item 3, p. 18](AAPL_2025_10K.pdf#page=21)
- **September 2 — Google search antitrust case:** Following the 2024 finding that Google had violated U.S. antitrust law, the D.C. district court ordered remedies. Apple said the order remained subject to further proceedings and appeal, and that potential remedies affecting Google’s search-distribution terms could materially affect Apple’s licensing revenue. [Risk Factors, p. 14](AAPL_2025_10K.pdf#page=17)
- **October — Epic Games appeal:** The Ninth Circuit heard oral arguments on Apple’s expedited appeal of the California district court’s April decision. Apple’s request to stay that decision pending appeal had been denied. [Item 3, p. 18](AAPL_2025_10K.pdf#page=21)

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2026 Form 10-K gives these goodwill amounts:

| Amount | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$20.832 billion** | Total goodwill on the consolidated balance sheet at January 25, 2026, rounded to $20.8 billion in Note 5. |
| **$20.5 billion** | Goodwill allocated to the Compute & Networking reporting unit at January 25, 2026. |
| **$370 million** | Goodwill allocated to the Graphics reporting unit at January 25, 2026. |
| **$15.6 billion** | Goodwill added during fiscal 2026, all allocated to Compute & Networking. |
| **$14.4 billion** | Goodwill recorded in connection with the Groq technology license and hiring of certain Groq employees. It was primarily attributable to the workforce and future development of the licensed technology, allocated to Compute & Networking, and tax deductible. |

The $14.4 billion Groq amount is **part of**, not additional to, the fiscal 2026 increase. NVIDIA reported no goodwill impairment in its fiscal 2026 annual test. [NVIDIA fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, pp. 53, 61, 63]

The filing says the initial effects of COVID-19 on commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers were particularly severe. In reassessing PCC, Berkshire considered airlines’ announcements about future demand, employment levels and aircraft orders; manufacturers’ announcements of reduced aircraft production; and restructuring actions Berkshire was taking or might take.

Given those circumstances, Berkshire increased the discount rates and reduced its prior long-term cash-flow forecasts used in its impairment review. Those changes reduced estimated fair values, leading to the charges where carrying values exceeded fair values. The filing notes that PCC had historically derived significant revenue and earnings from aerospace products. [Berkshire Hathaway 2021 Form 10-K, pp. K-48, K-62–K-63]

Boeing distinguishes the **strike** from the **new collective bargaining agreement**:

- **Employees:** IAM District 837 represented approximately **3,200 Boeing employees** at its St. Louis-area sites. This is the represented-employee count, not an explicitly stated count of employees who struck.
- **Strike:** The work stoppage began **August 4, 2025**, and lasted **101 days**. On **November 13, 2025**, District 837 members voted to ratify a new contract, ending the stoppage.
- **Current agreement:** Boeing lists **July 2030** as the expiration date of its principal District 837 agreement, whose principal location is Missouri. The filing does not give an exact expiration day or explicitly state the agreement’s term in years.

Source: Boeing 2025 Form 10-K, pp. 2 and 24 (PDF pp. 4 and 26).

Pfizer attributed the increase mainly to its 2022 acquisitions of **Arena, Global Blood Therapeutics (GBT), and Biohaven**. It provisionally recorded $5.0 billion, $3.0 billion, and $450 million, respectively, in acquired IPR&D assets. [Pfizer 2022 Form 10-K, pp. 59–60, 79]

The increase was partly offset by a **$200 million impairment** of an IPR&D asset acquired with Array. The asset concerned an unapproved treatment for symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy caused by a mutation in the gene encoding the lamin A/C protein. Pfizer said the impairment resulted from the Phase 3 trial reaching futility at a pre-planned interim analysis. [Pfizer 2022 Form 10-K, p. 67]

Apple identifies several causes of quarter-to-quarter differences in net sales:

- **Seasonal demand:** Sales have historically been higher in the first fiscal quarter, partly because of holiday demand.
- **Product and service introductions:** Their timing can significantly affect sales. Indirect channels build inventory after a launch and often reduce inventory of an older product as its replacement approaches. Consumer and distributor anticipation can also affect sales.
- **Demand concentration:** Apple generates a significant portion of sales from a single product, so a decline in demand for it could significantly affect quarterly sales.
- **Unexpected developments:** These include lower-than-anticipated demand, problems with launches, IT system failures or network disruptions, and failures by logistics, component-supply or manufacturing partners.

The filing also notes that an **extra week is added to the first fiscal quarter** every five or six years; this occurred in fiscal 2023. (Apple 2023 Form 10-K, pp. 4, 15 and 20.)

Walmart’s fiscal 2022 Form 10-K gives these Flipkart-linked figures:

- **$3.2 billion:** Amount Walmart received in fiscal 2022 primarily from new equity funding for Flipkart. The funding reduced Walmart’s ownership from approximately **83%** at January 31, 2021, to approximately **75%**. Exhibit 21 also lists Walmart’s Flipkart equity ownership as **75%**. [pp. 43, 64, 164]
- **$2.2 billion:** Cash at January 31, 2022 that Walmart could access only through dividends or intercompany financing arrangements subject to Flipkart minority-shareholder approval. Walmart expected Flipkart to use the cash. [p. 42]
- **$0.4 billion:** Fiscal 2020 Walmart International impairment charges consisting primarily of the write-off of Flipkart fashion trade name Jabong.com, following a decision to focus on Myntra.com. This is the stated charge, not a separately quantified Jabong-only amount. [p. 71]

The filing reports the **$3.2 billion** as *primarily* related to Flipkart, rather than entirely attributable to it.

The filing gives these **PTC-specific balances at December 31, 2023**:

| Amount | What it represents |
|---:|---|
| **$21.404 billion** | PTC segment identifiable assets at year-end. |
| **$6.605 billion** | PTC segment goodwill at year-end. |
| **Approximately $6.6 billion** | PTC’s portion of the net carrying value of railroad, utilities and energy other intangible assets. |
| **Approximately $2.1 billion** | PTC’s portion of railroad, utilities and energy receivables. |
| **Approximately $1.7 billion** | PTC’s portion of railroad, utilities and energy inventories, materials and supplies. |
| **$5.776 billion** | Notes payable and other borrowings of PTC and subsidiaries, due 2024–2028. |

The identifiable-assets figure excludes goodwill in the segment reconciliation; the listed receivables, inventories and intangible assets are components of assets, not additional amounts to add to identifiable assets. The debt is predominantly secured syndicated loans.

Source: Berkshire Hathaway 2023 Form 10-K, Notes 8–10, 13, 19 and 26, pp. K-88–89, K-91, K-102 and K-114.

For fiscal 2025, which ended January 26, 2025, NVIDIA reported the following investment gains and losses, in millions:

| Investment | Amount | What it represents |
|---|---:|---|
| Publicly held equities | **$163 gain** | Net unrealized gains for fiscal 2025 on securities held at period-end. |
| Publicly held equities | **$88 gain** | Net realized gains on securities sold, measured against their carrying value at the beginning of the period or their purchase date, if later. |
| Non-marketable equities | **$816 gain** | Unrealized gains recognized as adjustments to carrying value. |
| Non-marketable equities | **$59 loss** | Impairments and unrealized losses recognized as adjustments to carrying value. |
| Non-marketable equities | **$565 gain** | An unrealized gain from a private company’s secondary equity transaction in the fourth quarter. This is **part of**, not additional to, the $816 million above. |

The disclosed non-marketable unrealized gains less impairments and unrealized losses were therefore **$757 million net**. NVIDIA recognizes realized and unrealized gains and losses on these investments in other income or expense.

Source: [NVIDIA fiscal 2025 Form 10-K, pp. 66, 68–69](NVDA_2025_10K.pdf).

ExxonMobil’s 2024 Form 10-K gives these measures of Pioneer’s size and contribution:

| Measure | Figure | What it represents |
|---|---:|---|
